text: Hume denies that induction can be given a non-circular justification. Why, specifically, does he reject the attempt to justify induction by pointing out that it has worked reliably in the past?
choices: Because the conclusion of an inductive inference concerns a matter of fact, whose denial is never a contradiction, so the inference cannot be deductively valid.
Because the argument is deductively valid but unsound, since its premises are actually false.
Because induction has in fact frequently failed in the past, so the premise about its track record is empirically false.
Because such a justification presupposes that the future will resemble the past, the very inductive principle it is trying to justify, and so begs the question.
explanation: Appealing to induction's track record uses induction to justify induction: it assumes the uniformity of nature (that observed regularities extend to unobserved cases), which is exactly what is at issue, so the defense is circular. The option about a matter of fact's denial never being a contradiction is a genuine Humean point, but it explains why deduction cannot justify induction, not why the track-record defense fails.
